# Nehemiah Chapter 2 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 470v–471r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/NEH_002_page_001.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was set before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. I had never before appeared sad in his presence.

**2** The king said to me, "Why is your face sad, since you are not ill? This can only be sadness of heart." And I was very much afraid.

**3** I said to the king, "Let the king live forever! Why should my face not be sad, when the city — the place of my fathers' tombs — lies desolate, and its gates have been consumed by fire?"

**4** The king said to me, "What are you requesting?" So I prayed to the God of heaven.

**5** I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor before you, send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' tombs, that I may rebuild it."

**6** The king — with the queen sitting beside him — said to me, "How long will your journey take, and when will you return?" It pleased the king to send me, and I set him a time.

**7** I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let letters be given me for the governors of the province Beyond the River, that they may grant me passage until I reach Judah,

**8** and a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress by the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I shall occupy." The king granted my request, for the good hand of my God was upon me.

**9** I came to the governors of Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. The king had also sent officers of the army and horsemen with me.

**10** When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard of it, it greatly displeased them that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.

**11** I arrived in Jerusalem and was there three days.

**12** Then I rose in the night, I and a few men with me. I told no one what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me except the one I rode.

**13** I went out by night through the Valley Gate, past the Dragon Spring, and to the Dung Gate, inspecting the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been consumed by fire.

**14** I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal beneath me to pass.

**15** I went up along the valley by night, inspecting the wall, then turned back and entered through the Valley Gate, and so returned.

**16** The officials did not know where I had gone or what I had been doing. I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, or the rest who would do the work.

**17** Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in — Jerusalem lies desolate, its gates consumed by fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we may no longer be a disgrace."

**18** I told them how the hand of my God had been upon me for good, and also the words the king had spoken to me. They said, "Let us rise up and build!" And they strengthened their hands for the good work.

**19** But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite servant, and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they mocked us and despised us, saying, "What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?"

**20** I answered them, "The God of heaven will give us success. We his servants will rise up and build, but you have no portion, no right, and no memorial in Jerusalem."

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Nehemiah 2 transitions from prayer to action with remarkable narrative skill. The chapter divides into three movements: the royal audience (vv. 1-8), the secret night inspection (vv. 11-16), and the public call to rebuild (vv. 17-20). Theologically, the phrase "the good hand of my God" (v. 8) becomes a leitmotif throughout the book, attributing every success to divine providence working through human agency. The introduction of the three antagonists — Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem — establishes the external opposition that will drive much of the narrative tension.

---

## Disagreement Log

### V.3 — "tombs" vs. "graves" vs. "burial place"
- **EMET:** "graves" (*qivrot*) / **LOGOS:** "tombs" / **PNEUMA:** "graves"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "tombs" — Both "tombs" and "graves" are valid for *qivrot*; "tombs" carries slightly more architectural weight appropriate to ancestral burial in the ancient Near East.

### V.8 — "forest" vs. "royal forest" vs. "park"
- **EMET:** "king's-forest" (*ha-pardes*) / **LOGOS:** "king's forest" / **PNEUMA:** "royal forest"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "king's forest" — Retains the possessive construction of the Hebrew. The Persian loanword *pardes* means an enclosed park or forest; "forest" is adequate without adding "royal" (already implied by "the king's").

### V.20 — "memorial" vs. "claim" vs. "historic right"
- **EMET:** "no-memorial" (*zikkaron*) / **LOGOS:** "no claim" / **PNEUMA:** "no historic right"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "no memorial" — The Hebrew *zikkaron* specifically means a memorial or remembered legacy, not a legal claim. LOGOS and PNEUMA interpret rather than translate.

---

*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
